client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. I can't seem to focus at work at all — I'll be in the middle of something and then just completely lose my train of thought, and the sadness just hits me out of nowhere. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because it's not like anything can change what happened.
therapist:
I'm so sorry for the loss of your grandmother — what you're describing, those waves of grief that interrupt your day without warning, makes complete sense given how fresh this loss is. You're right that nothing can change what happened, and I'd never suggest otherwise; but talking can sometimes help us carry the weight of it differently, rather than feeling so alone under it. 

What was your grandmother like to you — what kind of presence did she have in your life?

client: She was honestly the one person in my life who never made me feel like I had to explain myself — I could just show up and she'd be glad to see me, no questions asked. We'd have tea every Sunday for years, and I didn't realize until she was gone how much that routine was kind of holding me together. Now Sundays feel unbearable, like there's this huge hole where something solid used to be.
therapist:
What a profound and irreplaceable gift she gave you — that kind of unconditional, no-explanation-needed acceptance is something so many people spend their whole lives searching for, and it makes complete sense that losing her feels like losing something structural, not just emotional. Those Sunday teas weren't just a routine; they were a place where you could simply *be*, and your mind and heart are grieving that anchor just as much as they're grieving her. 

I'm curious — when you sit with that feeling of the hole on Sundays now, what do you find yourself doing, or wishing you could do?

client: Mostly I just end up sitting there feeling guilty, like I should be doing something to honor her memory but I don't know what that would even look like. Last Sunday I tried calling my mom to talk about her, but it turned into this awkward conversation where we were both just kind of... not saying the real things, you know? I keep wishing I could just have one more Sunday with her, which I know is pointless to think about, but I can't seem to stop.
therapist:
That wish for one more Sunday isn't pointless at all — it's actually your mind's way of telling you exactly what you're missing and how much she mattered, and there's real meaning in that. The guilt you're feeling often comes from love that doesn't know where to go yet, rather than from anything you've actually done wrong. 

I wonder — when you imagine what "honoring her" might look like, does any small, quiet idea come to mind, even one that feels too simple or silly to say out loud?

client: There's this part of me that thinks I could make her tea on Sunday mornings the way she used to make it — she had this specific way she'd do it, with the saucer and everything — but then I think, what's the point, I'd just be sitting there alone feeling even worse. I guess I'm scared that doing something like that would just make the hole feel bigger instead of smaller. It's hard to explain, but trying to recreate something she's not part of anymore feels almost cruel to myself.
therapist:
That instinct to protect yourself from more pain makes complete sense, and it shows real self-awareness that you can name that fear so clearly. But I'm gently curious about something — you said it *might* make the hole feel bigger, and I wonder if part of you also senses it might do something else too, something harder to predict, which is maybe why the idea came to you at all. 

What do you think she would say if she knew you were considering making that cup of tea in her honor?

client: She'd probably laugh a little and tell me I was overthinking it, which is exactly the kind of thing she'd say. And honestly, just imagining her saying that made me feel something for a second — not just sadness, but something almost warm, which is strange. I don't know, maybe there's something to what you're saying, but I'm still not sure I can actually sit through that on my own without it just falling apart.
therapist:
That warm feeling you just described - that's not strange at all, that's *her*, still present in the way she shaped you and the way you carry her voice inside you. And I want to gently reflect back that you just did something brave: you imagined something painful, and instead of only finding hurt, you found a flicker of warmth too - which suggests the tea might hold both, not just loss. 

What if "falling apart" for a little while on a Sunday morning was actually allowed - not something to prevent, but something she might have quietly sat with you through anyway?

client: That actually hit me harder than I expected, because you're right — she was always the person I could fall apart in front of without feeling ashamed about it. I think part of what makes Sundays so hard is that I feel like I have to hold it together now because she's not there to make it okay to not be okay. I'm not saying I'm ready to try the tea thing this Sunday, but I'm not completely ruling it out either, which is maybe more than I could've said an hour ago.
therapist:
That shift you just described — from "I'm not sure talking will help" to "I'm not completely ruling it out" — is genuinely meaningful, and I don't want it to pass without acknowledging it. And what you've uncovered feels really important: that the hardest part of Sundays might not just be missing her, but suddenly having to be your own permission-giver to fall apart, when she was the one who made that safe. 

I'm wondering — is there any small way you might try to offer yourself a little of that same permission she used to give you, even just this week?

client: I think the honest answer is that I don't really know how to give myself permission for anything — I'm usually the person telling myself to push through and keep it together, so it feels almost foreign as a concept. I guess I could try to at least not fill Sunday with distractions on purpose, like maybe just let myself feel whatever comes up instead of immediately reaching for my phone or turning on the TV. But I'm a little worried that without someone like her there to make it feel safe, I'll just end up feeling lonelier than before.
therapist:
What you just described — choosing not to reach for a distraction — is actually a quiet, courageous act of self-permission, even if it doesn't feel that way yet, and it's a meaningful first step toward learning to be that gentle presence for yourself. Your worry about loneliness is real and worth honoring, but I'm also noticing that you've spent this last hour sitting with hard feelings without running from them, and something valuable came through anyway. 

What if this Sunday, even for just a few minutes, you tried treating yourself the way she would have — not demanding you hold it together, just letting yourself show up, no explanation needed?

client: That framing — treating myself the way she would have — is something I think I can actually hold onto, because it feels less like a task and more like something familiar. I'm still nervous about it, but I think the fear is a little smaller than it was when I walked in here today. I just hope I can remember that in the moment on Sunday when everything feels heavy and she's not there to remind me.
therapist:
The fact that it feels familiar rather than like a task tells me you already know how to do this somewhere inside you — she taught you what that care feels like, and that knowledge doesn't leave just because she did. And if Sunday feels heavy and you forget in the moment, that's okay too — you can even ask yourself, "what would she do right now?" and see what comes back to you, the way her voice came back just a little while ago when you imagined her laughing at you for overthinking. 

Would it feel helpful to come back and tell me how Sunday goes — whatever shape it takes?

client: Yeah, I think I'd like that — having somewhere to bring it afterward actually makes it feel a little less like I'm just going to be alone with it on Sunday. I'm still not promising myself I'll make the tea, but I think I'll at least try the thing where I ask what she'd do, because her voice did come back pretty easily just now and that surprised me. I didn't really expect to feel anything useful coming into this conversation today, so I guess that's something.
therapist:
That last line you just said — "I guess that's something" — I want to reflect it back to you, because it's actually quite a lot: you came in doubting this would help, and you're leaving with a piece of her voice, a small intention for Sunday, and somewhere to bring it afterward. She sounds like she'd be quietly pleased about that, maybe with a cup of tea and a saucer. 

I'll be here when you're ready to come back — and whatever Sunday brings, you won't be carrying it alone.

client: That image of her with the tea and the saucer actually made me smile, which feels strange and okay at the same time. I think I came in here expecting to just feel worse by talking about it, and instead I feel a little less like I'm drowning in it, which I didn't see coming. I'll try to hold onto that going into Sunday, and I think I'll come back and tell you how it goes — whatever that looks like.
therapist:
That smile is worth everything — it's grief and love living right next to each other, which is exactly where they belong, and there's nothing strange about that at all. You came in bracing for more weight and instead found a little breathing room, and that happened because you were willing to stay with the hard feelings long enough to find something real inside them. 

Take good care of yourself this week, and I'll be here Sunday — tea optional, but you're always welcome.
